# Introduction

RhyME is an R package for detecting circadian rhythms in DNA methylation
data. It fits beta-regression cosinor models to methylation beta values. The package supports independent samples and
repeated measurements from the same subjects, with optional covariates
such as age and sex. An empirical Bayes (EB) prior can improve the
stability of precision estimates across CpGs.

RhyME identifies rhythmic CpG sites and estimates their amplitude, peak
time, and mean methylation level. This vignette walks through installation,
data preparation, model fitting, viewing results, and plotting fitted curves.

# Installation

Install the package:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install("https://github.com/njuelsdke/RhyME")
```


# Load data

The bundled example contains 10,000 simulated CpGs from eight subjects,
each sampled six times.

```{r data}
library(RhyME)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(BiocParallel)

example <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "example_data.rds",
    package = "RhyME"))
se <- example$se
dim(se)
head(as.data.frame(colData(se)))
```

## Prepare your own data

Use a numeric matrix of beta values, with CpGs in rows and
samples in columns. Sample metadata should contain collection time in hours
and, for repeated measurements, a subject identifier. CpG and sample names
should be unique, sample names must match between the matrix and metadata.

For example, read two CSV files whose first columns contain row names:

```{r own-data, eval=FALSE}
beta <- as.matrix(read.csv("beta_values.csv", row.names = 1,
    check.names = FALSE))
sample_info <- read.csv("sample_metadata.csv", row.names = 1)
sample_info <- sample_info[colnames(beta), , drop = FALSE]

se <- SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(beta = beta),
    colData = DataFrame(sample_info))
```

Missing observations are allowed. Time, subject identifiers, and any
adjustment covariates should be complete.

# Fit the model

For repeated measurements, specify the time and subject columns. This
example fits all 10,000 CpGs with the EB prior:

```{r fit}
fit <- fitCosinor(se,
    time_col = "time", subject_col = "subject", assay_name = "beta",
    period = 24, prior = "auto",
    BPPARAM = SerialParam())
```

Set `period` to the rhythm length in hours; the default is 24. Sampling
times can be irregular or span several days. `prior = "auto"` estimates
an EB prior from the data and needs at least 1,000 usable CpGs. Use
`prior = "none"` for smaller datasets.

# View results

Results are stored in `rowData(fit)`. Sort by p-value to view the top CpGs:

```{r results}
result <- as.data.frame(rowData(fit))
result <- result[order(result$pvalue, na.last = NA), , drop = FALSE]
head(result[, c("amplitude", "phase", "mesor", "pvalue", "padj",
    "converged")], 10)
```

The beta value scale rhythm summaries below are population-averaged quantities, obtained by marginalizing over the fitted random-intercept distribution.

- `amplitude`: half the fitted peak-to-trough difference on the beta-value scale.
- `phase`: peak time in hours, between 0 and `period`, relative to the input time origin.
- `mesor`: fitted mean methylation level averaged over one period.



Select CpGs at a 5% false discovery rate:

```{r significant}
significant <- result[result$padj < 0.05, , drop = FALSE]
nrow(significant)
```

View the fitting summary and estimated EB prior:

```{r summary}
metadata(fit)$RhyME$fitSummary
metadata(fit)$RhyME$ebPrior
```

# Plot fitted curves

By default, `plotCosinorFit()` shows up to six CpGs with usable estimates,
ordered by p-value. Points are observed beta values and the red line is the
fitted mean curve.

```{r plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
plotCosinorFit(fit)
```

Select CpGs by name and set the number of panels per row:

```{r selected-plot, eval=FALSE}
plotCosinorFit(fit, cpgs = rownames(result)[1:3], ncol = 3)
```


# Other options

## Adjust for covariates

Add covariates to `colData(se)` and pass their column names. Numeric and
categorical variables are supported. Here we add example subject ages and
fit a small subset:

```{r covariates}
colData(se)$age <- rep(c(28, 42, 35, 51, 39, 47, 31, 55), each = 6)
adjusted <- fitCosinor(se[seq_len(50), ],
    time_col = "time", subject_col = "subject", covariates = "age",
    prior = "none", BPPARAM = SerialParam(), verbose = FALSE)
```

For multiple covariates, use `covariates = c("age", "sex")` when both
columns are present. Do not include the subject identifier as a covariate.


## Independent samples

For an object `se_independent` containing independent samples, omit
`subject_col` to use the fixed-effects model:

```{r fixed, eval=FALSE}
fit_fixed <- fitCosinor(se_independent,
    time_col = "time", assay_name = "beta", period = 24,
    prior = "none", BPPARAM = SerialParam())
```
